Chinatown's Lunch Spot Is Shut, a Medical Team Is on the Sidewalk, and the Roster Has Nothing to Say I was standing at a Chinatown corner when the medical team went past me. Timmie Hall was already on the curb. The lunch spot behind her was dark, with a notice taped to the door. "I've noticed some changes around here, like the lunch spot on the corner being closed suddenly," Hall told me. "And just now, there was a medical emergency on the sidewalk. It's not usually like that here."

Hall is a refugee resettlement case worker and lives and works in Chinatown. She knows what usual looks like here, and a small crowd gathered around a stranger on the pavement isn't it. Two doors down I found Mei Chen, who runs a gallery in the neighborhood. She had walked to the same lunch spot and found the same notice. "To be honest, it's a bit worrying to see some of our local businesses struggling," she said. "I've been going there for years. The medical emergency on the sidewalk doesn't help the vibe either."

Liliana Salazar: “I've seen the news about Chinatown, and to be honest, it doesn't surprise me. I've watched the fog roll over the port cranes from my front window, and it's made me think about how some parts of Oakland are changing while others seem stuck. I don't know what's going on with Chinatown, but it feels like it's been on a downward slide for a while. I haven't been there recently, but I've heard things from friends. It's a shame, really.” Wren Choi: “I've noticed some changes around my neighborhood, Glenview, lately. More people seem to be home during the day, and there's a bit of a different vibe. I haven't been to Chinatown recently, but I do hear things. It sounds like it's not doing great. I don't know what's going on there, but it makes me wonder if anyone is paying attention to it.”

I asked two people in Glenview what they'd heard. Neither has been to Chinatown lately. Liliana Salazar is an EV mechanic. Elle Lilo stepped back onto the bridge at Jack London, the first time in weeks her boots had met the metal grating without the weight of a lingering cough in her chest. The tugs moved below as they always did, horns cutting across the water, but the air felt different with the cranes sharp against the sky and gulls wheeling without the usual gray press.

Elle Lilo: “Three clear days in a row — that's a gift around here. When I finally shook that cold, the first morning I stepped back on the bridge, the sky was wide open, and I swear I could feel it in my chest. The work doesn't change, not really — the tugs still pull, the horns still sound — but the day feels lighter. You can see the whole bay, the cranes, the gulls, all of it. It's like the harbor is breathing again, and so am I.” Rafael Brannie: “Three clear days helps, sure. I noticed the light today walking to the job—it's different, makes you want to linger on the corner a moment longer. But the winter mood, that's a heavier coat than the weather. It kind of stays draped on you even when the sun's out. I haven't gone out of my way to see people yet. I'm still moving, working, that part doesn't stop. But sitting with someone, sharing a beer, that takes a little more than blue sky. The mood outlasts the weather, I think. The sun gets you halfway there, the rest is on you.”

I've been around the block with Rayon Dart, and we talk about stuff like this. He's seen it before. I just need to stay focused and keep doing what I'm doing.” Adash Stanley: “When the role changes, the record doesn't care who's carrying it. It just sits there at 2-0 and asks the next guy to keep it honest. For me, that means showing up the same way I always have — steady, ready, not making it about me. The continuity is in the work, not the title.” Austin Reaves: “Look, 2-0 feels good, don't get me wrong. But I've been around long enough to know a record doesn't hold the building up. It's the guys inside it. We're still figuring out who we are out there — roles, rotations, all that. The structure shifting? That's just part of the game. You don't carry the weight by pretending everything's locked in. You carry it by showing up, doing your job, and trusting the guys next to you. That's what I'm doing. That's all I can do.” Adash Stanley: “The mood among fans is electric. I've felt the excitement building around the Oaks, it's like the whole city is waking up with the team. Maybe they're finally getting their act together.” Austin Reaves: “To be honest, the neighborhood's been buzzing about the Oaks' 4-0 start. I've seen fans around here getting really excited, and it's infectious. People are talking about it while they're out and about, like when they're unloading groceries or just hanging out on their stoops. The mood feels hungry for more, like they're really craving the next win. I've even noticed some folks around here discussing the team's defense and how well they're working together. It's great to see the community coming together like this behind the team.” Desmond Morton: “Honestly, the coaches haven't given me a clear answer yet.
